component.name: Bars
component.summary: Private, on-device voice dictation for every app

description.p: Hold a shortcut, speak, and let go: Bars transcribes your voice with a fast local speech model and types the text into whatever app you are using. Nothing is sent over the network.

ul.li: Push-to-talk or hands-free dictation from a global shortcut
NVIDIA Parakeet and Canary models running on your CPU via ONNX Runtime
Removes filler words, supports a personal dictionary and snippets
Lives in the system tray with a minimal recording indicator

Linux: Update now installs the new version in place, then asks whether to restart Bars. This works for the release tarball (if Bars can write to its folder) and for the release Flatpak (installed for your user); other copies still open the release page. Updating this way starts after this version, so install this one by hand.
Restarting into an update waits until you've finished dictating, and Bars says so if it can't restart itself.
Long dictations paste as text, not a collapsed placeholder, in Droid, pi and OpenCode too, besides Claude Code and Codex. The setting is now called Split long pastes for coding agents.
Coding agents running in a herdr pane are found too.

macOS 27: Bars no longer says it needs Device Control and Data Access when it already has it and works. Some Macs report the permission as off while it's on; Bars now also checks what it can actually do.

The Setup page speaks each system's language: on macOS it asks for the microphone and Accessibility (Device Control and Data Access on macOS 27), on Windows for the microphone, and on Linux for the microphone and keyboard access. Its status shows how Bars sees your shortcut, types and treats the clipboard on your system.
macOS: Setup shows whether Bars may put back what you had copied, with Allow… when macOS asks first. Bars says it lives in the menu bar.
macOS: bars --doctor and the log show each permission check on its own.

macOS 27: macOS now asks before an app reads the clipboard, and its Allow lasts a single read. Bars no longer reads the clipboard unless it's allowed, so the clipboard can't end up empty: until then it keeps your dictation instead of what you had copied. To get your copied things back after each dictation, click Allow… next to Restore clipboard in settings, then turn on Bars under Privacy & Security › Paste from Other Apps.
macOS 27: setup and messages call the Accessibility permission by its new name, Device Control and Data Access.
macOS: Bars is signed with an Apple Developer ID and notarized by Apple, so it opens without a warning, with no “Open Anyway” in Privacy & Security.

macOS: because of the new signature, macOS asks once more for Microphone and Accessibility access (and System Audio Recording, if Bars mutes other apps). If Bars is already listed and switched on in Accessibility, remove it with the − button and add it again. From then on the permissions last through updates.

macOS: fixes Bars getting stuck, with no start sound and then “Couldn't finish the recording”, when the microphone and the speakers are one audio device, like a USB interface. Bars no longer changes that device's buffer size.
If the audio device stops responding anyway, Bars keeps what it recorded and says so. On macOS it then restarts itself.
macOS: Bars keeps a log in ~/Library/Logs/Bars.log.

Output polish keeps a clean-up that writes an ordinal as digits, like “the fifteenth” as “the 15th”, instead of dropping it. A clean-up that breaks lines you didn't say is dropped, so it can't send a message early. AM or PM after a 24-hour time (“15:15 PM”) is left out.

A shortcut can be a single key, like F9 or Pause, or a modifier on its own, like Right Option or Right Ctrl. Recording one remembers which side you pressed, so the other side works as usual. Keys that type or edit text, and Escape, still need a modifier.
Mute other audio now works on macOS 14.2 and later. It takes the System Audio Recording permission, which macOS asks for when you turn the option on; Bars never records.

Long dictations are transcribed while you talk: Bars cuts them at pauses and transcribes and polishes each piece in the background, so the text goes in moments after you stop. Dictations under 12 seconds work as before.
Fixes long dictations that came out empty: getting a long recording ready could take longer than Bars waited for it.
Mute other audio (Microphone settings, off by default) silences music, videos and other apps while you dictate, and turns them back on after.
Bars looks for updates when it starts and every 24 hours while it runs, counting the time the computer sleeps.
The licenses of the open-source software Bars is built with come with every package, and the settings link to them.
More than one shortcut: Add shortcut in Shortcut & input records another, and they all start dictation the same way. At least one always stays.

A shortcut can be a mouse button: the middle button or a side or extra button (Mouse 3, Mouse 4, Mouse 5...), on its own or with modifiers. Left and right click can't be shortcuts, and clicking never gets in the way of one.
On macOS and Windows a mouse-button shortcut does nothing else in the app. On Linux it also reaches the app, and Bars asks once more for access to mice.
Home shows every shortcut.

Output polish: English dictations are cleaned up on this computer by a small model, Spokenly Cleanup 1 by Spokenly. Filler words, repeats and false starts go, spoken corrections like "no wait" are applied, and numbers, email and web addresses are written as you'd type them. Questions and instructions stay as you said them.
Output polish is on by default. Setup downloads its model (639 MB) after the speech model; if you had Bars before, it asks once.
Output polish reads the app and the text around the cursor while you're still talking, so less is left to do after you stop.
On PCs, Output polish needs a processor with AVX2 (Intel since 2013, AMD since 2015).
The Speech model page is now Models, with Output polish below the speech models.
Model downloads wait their turn instead of being refused while another one runs.
The settings window reaches the top edge, without a line under the title bar.

Dictations fit into the text around the cursor: a space only where one is needed, lowercase when continuing a sentence, and no full stop when the sentence carries on (in apps with accessibility support).
When no text box has focus, Bars says so and offers the text to copy.
Pasted text stays out of clipboard-history apps, and everything you had copied (images and files too) comes back afterwards.
Long text pasted into Claude Code or Codex goes in pieces, so it shows as text instead of "[Pasted text]".
Escape cancels a hands-free dictation without also reaching the app.
A key release Bars missed no longer blocks the shortcut.
With a Parakeet model, Bars learns from your corrections: fix a word it got wrong and it's added to your dictionary, with Undo. Less clear fixes wait under Suggestions.
Dictations can be corrected on the History page.
Bars looks for a new version once a day and tells you; it's installed only when you choose Update (on Linux the release page opens). The check can be turned off.
Parakeet hears short phrases it used to return nothing for.
macOS: the text around the cursor is also read in rich text editors on web pages.
macOS: the app icon has the same shape as other Mac apps.
macOS: the app is signed, so a downloaded copy no longer reports itself as damaged, and permissions are kept across updates.
macOS: Bars shows in the Dock while its settings are open.
Model downloads trust the system's certificates, so they work behind company proxies and antivirus that inspect HTTPS.
macOS: changing the shortcut works again; the shortcut keeps working after macOS asks for a password, and with Caps Lock on.
The version is shown in the settings sidebar and by bars --version.
macOS: switching microphones no longer freezes Bars, and Bars no longer changes the microphone's format for other apps.
The setup assistant's microphone check lets you pick another microphone.
With "Save history" off, dictations are no longer recorded anywhere, and transcripts stay out of the logs.
macOS: no longer crashes when inserting text after dictation.
macOS: setup asks only for Accessibility, and Allow access opens its settings.
macOS: the disk image shows its background and layout again.
Arm64 builds for Linux and Windows are paused.

description.p: Windows and macOS: global shortcut, typing and pasting, tray, setup assistant, launch at login, and the dictation pill.

ul.li: macOS: Fn (Globe) works as a shortcut; menu-bar app without a Dock icon.
Arm64 builds for Linux and Windows.
The setup assistant notices permissions granted in system settings.
